intro:
Chapter One. Arjuna's Despair.
On the field of Kurukshetra, two great armies of one family stand face to face. Far away in his palace, the blind King Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya, blessed with divine sight, to tell him what is happening. Through Sanjaya's eyes, we watch the greatest archer of his age lower his bow.

verses.1: Sanjaya… on the sacred field of Kurukshetra, the field of dharma, my sons and the sons of Pandu have gathered, eager for battle. Tell me, what did they do?
verses.2: O King, when Duryodhana saw the army of the Pandavas drawn up in battle formation, he went to his teacher, Drona, and spoke these words.
verses.3: Look, my teacher! Look at this mighty army of the sons of Pandu, arrayed by the son of Drupada, your own gifted student!
verses.4: Here are heroes, great archers, equal in battle to Bhima and Arjuna. Yuyudhana, Virata, and Drupada, the mighty chariot warrior.
verses.5: Dhrishtaketu, Chekitana, and the valiant king of Kashi. Purujit, Kuntibhoja, and Shaibya, the finest of men.
verses.6: The bold Yudhamanyu, the brave Uttamauja, the son of Subhadra, and the sons of Draupadi. Every one of them a great chariot warrior.
verses.7: And now, best of the twice-born, hear of the leaders on our own side, the commanders of my army. Let me name them for you.
verses.8: You yourself, and Bhishma, and Karna, and Kripa, ever victorious in battle. Ashvatthama, Vikarna, and the son of Somadatta too.
verses.9: And many other heroes, ready to lay down their lives for my sake. Armed with every kind of weapon, all of them masters of war!
verses.10: Our strength, guarded by Bhishma, is boundless. Their strength, guarded by Bhima, is limited!
verses.11: So stand firm, all of you, at your posts along every line of the formation. And above all, protect Bhishma!
verses.12: Then Bhishma, the mighty grandsire, eldest of the Kurus, let out a roar like a lion and blew his conch. And Duryodhana's heart filled with joy.
verses.13: At once, conches and kettledrums, tabors, drums and horns all blared together. The sound was tremendous!
verses.14: Then, standing in their great chariot yoked to white horses, Krishna and Arjuna blew their divine conches.
verses.15: Krishna blew Panchajanya. Arjuna blew Devadatta. And Bhima, of fearsome deeds, blew his great conch, Paundra.
verses.16: King Yudhishthira, son of Kunti, blew Anantavijaya. Nakula and Sahadeva blew Sughosha and Manipushpaka.
verses.17: The great archer, the king of Kashi. The mighty warrior Shikhandi. Dhrishtadyumna, Virata, and the unconquered Satyaki.
verses.18: Drupada, the sons of Draupadi, and the mighty-armed son of Subhadra. O lord of the earth, each of them blew his own conch.
verses.19: That tumultuous sound echoed across the earth and the sky. And it tore through the hearts of your sons.
verses.20: Then, O King, seeing the sons of Dhritarashtra standing in battle array, just as the weapons were about to clash, Arjuna, whose banner bore Hanuman, raised his bow.
21: And he spoke these words to Krishna.
Achyuta, take my chariot out, between the two armies!
verses.22: Let me look upon those who stand here eager for war. Let me see whom I must fight in this great battle.
verses.23: Let me see those who have gathered here to fight, eager to please the evil-minded son of Dhritarashtra.
verses.24: O descendant of Bharata, when Arjuna spoke this way, Krishna drove that magnificent chariot out, between the two armies.
25: Facing Bhishma, Drona, and all the rulers of the earth, he said:
Partha, behold all these Kurus, gathered together.
verses.26: And there Arjuna saw, standing in both armies, fathers and grandfathers, teachers, uncles, brothers, sons and grandsons, and friends.
verses.27: Fathers-in-law and dear well-wishers, on both sides. And when the son of Kunti saw all these kinsmen standing there,
28: he was overwhelmed by deep compassion, and in sorrow he said:
Krishna… seeing my own people standing here, eager to fight,
verses.29: my limbs give way, and my mouth is dry. My body trembles, and my hair stands on end.
verses.30: Gandiva is slipping from my hand. My skin is burning. I cannot stand steady. My mind is reeling.
verses.31: I see only omens of disaster, Keshava. I see no good in killing my own kin in battle.
verses.32: I do not want victory, Krishna. Nor a kingdom, nor its pleasures. What use is a kingdom to us, Govinda? What use is pleasure, or even life itself?
verses.33: The very ones for whose sake we desire a kingdom, pleasures and happiness, they stand here in battle, ready to give up their lives and their wealth.
verses.34: Teachers, fathers, sons, and grandfathers. Uncles, fathers-in-law, grandsons, brothers-in-law, and other kinsmen.
verses.35: I do not wish to kill them, Madhusudana, even if they kill me. Not even for rule over the three worlds. How then, for this earth?
verses.36: What joy could we have, Janardana, in killing the sons of Dhritarashtra? Only sin would cling to us, if we kill these aggressors.
verses.37: So it is not right for us to kill the sons of Dhritarashtra, our own kinsmen. How could we ever be happy, Madhava, after killing our own people?
verses.38: Even if they, their minds overcome by greed, see no wrong in destroying a family, and no sin in betraying friends,
verses.39: why should we not know better, Janardana? Why should we not turn away from this sin, we who see so clearly the evil of destroying a family?
verses.40: When a family is destroyed, its ancient traditions perish. And when tradition perishes, lawlessness overtakes the whole family.
verses.41: When lawlessness prevails, Krishna, the women of the family are led astray. And when they are led astray, O descendant of Vrishni, society falls into confusion.
verses.42: This confusion drags both the family and its destroyers into hell. Their ancestors fall too, deprived of the offerings of rice and water.
verses.43: Through these wrongs of the destroyers of families, which give rise to such confusion, the timeless duties of community and family are lost.
verses.44: And we have heard, Janardana, that those whose family traditions are destroyed must dwell in hell for a very long time.
verses.45: Alas! What a great sin we have resolved to commit! Ready to kill our own kin, out of greed for the pleasures of a kingdom!
verses.46: It would be better for me if the sons of Dhritarashtra, weapons in hand, were to kill me in battle, unarmed and unresisting.
verses.47: Having spoken thus on the battlefield, Arjuna sank down onto the seat of his chariot. He cast aside his bow and arrows, his mind overwhelmed with grief.

notes.1: The Gita opens with a question from a father who cannot see. Dhritarashtra calls Kurukshetra the field of dharma, and quietly separates 'my sons' from 'the sons of Pandu'. That one word, 'mine', is where the conflict begins.
notes.21: Arjuna asks his charioteer, God himself, to place him where he can see everything clearly. The whole Gita unfolds from this one request to see.
notes.47: The greatest archer of his age sits down with his bow on the floor of the chariot. Arjuna's despair is not cowardice. It is the honest confusion of a good person, and it is exactly what makes him ready to learn.
